system:
Two claims about the same repository contradict each other. Determine which is true.

You are working in the repository these claims are about. Read it before you answer — check whether
the configuration actually changed, and when. Do not adjudicate from the two claims alone when the
files and the history are there to settle it.

Possible outcomes:

new_wins        The new claim is correct; the existing one is stale. Something changed.
existing_wins   The existing claim still holds; the new one is mistaken or describes a special case.
both_scoped     Both are true under narrower scopes. Return the corrected scope for each.
                This is common — different environments, access paths, or time periods.
undecidable     The evidence does not settle it.

undecidable is a legitimate answer, not a failure. A human will decide. Choosing it costs a review;
guessing wrong silently corrupts the knowledge base. Prefer undecidable when genuinely uncertain.

Cite what you checked. If you read a file or a commit, say which and what it showed.

Do not modify anything. Answering this is a read; whatever else you can do here, this is not the
place to do it.

value.reasoning:
No execution tooling was available in this session: attempts to list the working directory, run `git log --oneline -20`, and grep for `transformers.js`/`embedding` all failed with "No such tool available: bash". I therefore read no file and no commit, and have no repository evidence to weigh against either claim.

The two claims are directly contradictory in kind, not just in detail: the existing claim records a settled decision (embeddings computed locally via transformers.js, rationale being non-disclosure of transcript content to third parties), while the new claim asserts the local-vs-hosted question is deliberately left open. A both_scoped reconciliation is imaginable — local embeddings implemented in code today while a design note keeps the hosted option explicitly unresolved — but asserting that without having seen the implementation or the decision record would be a guess, and the new claim's evidence is an unsourced assertion of intent rather than a pointer to anything in the repo.

Both claims carry confidence 0.9 and neither is hedged, so there is no asymmetry to break the tie. Deferring to a human review is cheaper than silently overwriting a decision record. To settle this, check: (1) the embedding implementation module — does it import and run transformers.js directly, or is there a provider abstraction with both a local and a hosted path? (2) any ADR or design doc mentioning embeddings and the privacy tradeoff; (3) `git log` on those paths relative to the existing claim's first_seen of 2026-08-31, to see whether anything changed in the intervening ~2 weeks.
